title: Cambrian explosion
description: Period of major evolutionary diversification of animal life
wiki_lead:
The Cambrian explosion (also known as the Cambrian radiation or Cambrian diversification) is a major evolutionary radiation event of the Earth's lifeforms beginning approximately 538.8 million years ago in the early Cambrian period of the Paleozoic era, during which a sudden diversification of complex life occurred in the fossil record. The radiations occurred following the Baykonurian glaciation and the End-Ediacaran extinction and marked a significantly different faunal pattern from the earlier Ediacaran biota, with fossil evidence from this period containing all five modern metazoan (animal) phyla, implying the first major radiation of all these clades except the poriferans (i.e. sponges, which first appeared much earlier at least during the preceding Ediacaran period and possibly as early as the Tonian period). It lasted between 13 million and 25 million years before ending at the Sinsk Event, and resulted in the divergence of most extant eumetazoan phyla.
Before early Cambrian diversification, most organisms were relatively simple soft-bodied marine life composed of individual cells or small multicellular clusters, occasionally organized into colonies. Majority of the Precambrian metazoans that radiated during the preceding Avalon explosion (i.e. the Ediacaran biota) were simple-bodied, sessile filter feeders (e.g. the frondomorphs) or relatively sedentary epibenthic microbivores (e.g. the proarticulates and trilobozoans); while a large portion of the Cambrian faunae were far more mobile bottom feeders and demersal nektons with far more complex body plans, most notably the presence of neurons and similar excitable cells. The Cambrian substrate revolution, which was marked by oxidative degradation of the organic microbial mat due to increased burrowing by endobenthic bilaterians into the seabed, further catalyzed the ecological succession by selecting organisms more capable of motility, bioerosion and predation. As the subsequent evolutionary arms race accelerated the rate of diversification, speciation became more complex and the variety of life began to resemble that seen today, with notable phyla including arthropods (most notably trilobites and dinocaridids), lophophorates (brachiopods and bryozoans), cnidarians (jellyfish and corals), echinoderms, vetulicolians and earliest chordates such as Pikaia, Yunnanozoon and Cathaymyrus, which later gave rise to lancelets, tunicates and early vertebrates such as the myllokunmingiids. The event was also accompanied by major diversification in other groups of organisms such as phytoplanktons and calcimicrobes.
The Cambrian explosion coincided with the evolution of mineralized tissues and skeletons, which are fossilizable and thus contributed greatly to the "explosive" abundance of fossil evidence in the early Cambrian while earlier Precambrian fossils are mostly mold, trace or chemical fossils instead of fossils proper. This had once led the academic society to mistakenly assume that no complex life had existed until they all "suddenly appeared" during the Cambrian, as seen by the term Phanerozoic (from Ancient Greek φανερός phanerós + ζωή zōḗ, meaning "visible life") coined in 1930 by the American geologist George Halcott Chadwick (1876–1953).

History and significance

The seemingly rapid appearance of fossils in the "Primordial Strata" was noted by William Buckland in the 1840s. Charles Darwin in his 1859 book On the Origin of Species discussed the then inexplicable lack of earlier fossils as one of the main difficulties for his theory of descent with slow modification through natural selection. The long-running puzzlement about the seemingly sudden appearance of the Cambrian fauna without evident precursor(s) centers on three key points: whether there really was a mass diversification of complex organisms over a relatively short period during the early Cambrian, what might have caused such rapid change, and what it would imply about the origin of animal life. Interpretation
grok_lead: The Cambrian explosion refers to a pivotal evolutionary event in Earth's history, occurring approximately 541 to 530 million years ago during the early Cambrian period, when the majority of major animal phyla suddenly appeared in the fossil record, representing a dramatic increase in biological diversity and the emergence of complex multicellular life forms. This relatively brief interval, lasting about 10 to 20 million years, witnessed the rapid evolution of animals with mineralized hard parts, such as exoskeletons and shells, enabling the preservation of diverse body plans including bilaterians, arthropods, echinoderms, mollusks, and chordates. Exceptional fossil deposits, notably the Burgess Shale in British Columbia, Canada, and the Chengjiang biota in China, provide critical evidence of this diversification, preserving not only hard-bodied organisms like trilobites and brachiopods but also soft-bodied forms such as worms, sponges, and early relatives of modern phyla, highlighting an unprecedented ecological complexity in marine environments. Prior to this event, life in the late Ediacaran period (around 575â541 million years ago) featured simpler, often soft-bodied organisms, suggesting that the explosion built upon Precambrian evolutionary foundations but accelerated dramatically at the Ediacaran-Cambrian boundary. The causes of the Cambrian explosion remain a subject of ongoing research and debate among paleontologists, with proposed drivers including a modest rise in atmospheric and shallow ocean oxygen levels around 539â538 million years ago, which may have facilitated larger body sizes and metabolic demands of active animals; ecological factors like predator-prey interactions and niche expansion; and genetic innovations in developmental biology. Recent analyses indicate a two-phase structure to the event: an initial phase from about 560 to 513 million years ago dominated by stem-group lineages (ancestral forms of major phyla), followed by a second phase of crown-group (modern-like) radiations after the Sinsk extinction event around 513 million years ago, which selectively eliminated earlier stem groups and paved the way for dominant clades; 2025 studies further suggest the diversification may have begun up to 15 million years earlier based on trace fossils and new soft-bodied discoveries. This event fundamentally shaped the trajectory of life on Earth, establishing the foundational diversity of animal lineages that persist today and influencing subsequent evolutionary patterns through the Phanerozoic eon.
